results.abstract: a similar relationship to the past as Sebald’s narrators, for example, Gestermann makes the claim that the historical materialist’s view of the past is primarily an individual and subjective one: “Der unbestreitbare Fokus des historischen Materialismus auf eine Betrachtung der Vergangenheit, die sich am subjektiven Blick der Einzelperson ausrichtet, entspricht ganz der erzählerischen Haltung Sebalds und der Perspektive seiner personalen Erzählerinstanzen” (71; similar claims appear throughout the book). The engagement with the past that Benjamin promotes, however, is clearly one meant to operate on a collective level. As Michael Löwy writes in Fire Alarm: Reading Walter Benjamin’s “On the Concept of History,” “The only possible Messiah is a collective one [ . . . ]. It is not a question of waiting for the Messiah [ . . . ] but of acting collectively” (trans. Chris Turner, Verso 2005: 33). Moreover, in applying Benjamin’s ideas to Sebald’s works, Gestermann often elides a key distinction: that between the individual’s memory of personal experiences and the collective memory of historical events in which individuals may participate. While it may be fruitful to move Benjamin’s ideas about the commemoration of the historical past onto new ground by applying them to personal memory, not to acknowledge the act of translation this involves is to exaggerate the parallel between the two writers’ subjects. Limited by the narrowness of its focus and by these faulty claims, Vergegenwärtigung der Vergangenheit constitutes a minor contribution to scholarship on W.G. Sebald.
